newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-The Bundesbank has shot its bolt - J.Pfister.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-The Bundesbank has shot its bolt - J.Pfister.

text.p: By Juergen Pfister, Senior Economist at Commerzbank AG
The Bundesbank has shot its bolt!

The publication of the January employment figures will strengthen the call for further interest rate reductions by the Bundesbank. Indicators from industry and retail trade are also showing that the strong increase in overall production in the second and third quarter of last year did not continue into the final quarter. At most, we expect a slight increase in real gross domestic product for the start of 1997 so that over the next few months the image of a weak economy will dominate in the minds of the public at large and in the financial markets.

There are doubtless central bank council representatives who sympathise with a policy of economic fine-tuning. They point at growing unemployment, at under-utilisation of capacity, at low wage increases and the slowing effect of state consolidation in Germany and in many of our neighbouring countries in western Europe. In such an environment, so the argument goes, expansive monetary policy holds no dangers for the value of money. If the Bundesbank were to share these views, however, it would have to cut money market rates strongly -- 20 basis points on the securities repurchase rate would not be enough.

However, we think it is highly unlikely that the Bundesbank will increase the degree of expansionism in its policy. In doing so it would be giving up its own concept, the formative strength of which has already been diminished in the last few years. Further reductions in interest rates in Germany and in our neighbouring countries might perhaps help the candidates for monetary union to clear the hurdles set by the entrance examination in spring 1998. They would, however, also bring considerable risks for the initial phase of joint monetary policy.

Above all, three things speak against a relaxation of monetary policy in the present circumstances. Firstly: Monetary policy is already expansive and has been for some time, and fully takes advantage of the scope allowed by a medium-term orientated concept. There is hardly any dissent in the diagnosis of the weak economy: the spark from exports is not spreading to corporate investment. In addition the construction industry is undergoing structural adjustments. Lower interest rates or an expansive monetary policy cannot help here.

Secondly: The deutschemark has suffered a significant loss in value in the currency markets. In the phase when the deutschemark was strong the upward revaluation was brought into play as a reason for interest rate cuts; conversely when the deutschemark has a lower value in the currency markets, the monetary situation also stimulates the economy without further interest rate reductions. Even if the exchange rate development expresses the strength of the American economy and the corresponding increase in interest rates as well as the insecurities about the euro, the devaluation signals to the Bundesbank that further interest rate steps could quickly lead to dangerous excesses in the currency markets.

Thirdly: The trend in prices is heading upwards again. Even if the influences in the rate of inflation caused by the weather in January are taken into account, a rate approaching the two percent mark must be expected in the course of the year. Furthermore, higher wage increases are looming for 1998; following several years of offering relief, the import prices are providing a headwind. All this is not dramatic. However, the impression that there are still no signs of a risk of inflation misses the point. Today's monetary policy decisions affect the trend in prices in 1999, which will be attributed by the public to the European Central Bank. For this reason a further cut in interest rates by the Bundesbank would appear to represent stronger evidence for the suspicion expressed every now and then that the Bundesbank takes a critical view of monetary union rather than the refusal to cut rates.

These considerations lead us to believe that the Bundesbank will leave the repo rate at three percent for the next few months. If buoyant forces have made their mark in the economy by the spring, the Bundesbank will use the remaining time up to determination of the participants in monetary union to introduce a "gentle" corrective price adjustment, that is to switch from expansive to neutral. In spring 1998 the German money market interest rates will be around 50 basis points higher than at the moment. Economic recovery and maintenance of the market expectation that monetary union will start on time are central to this scenario.

Dr. Juergen Pfister is Senior Economist at Commerzbank AG. The author accepts sole responsibility for the contents of this article. The translation from the German language into English was carried out by Reuters.
